key_concept: Each vitamin has a characteristic dietary source: vitamin A from carrots (as $\beta$-carotene), $B_{12}$ from animal foods such as meat, E from vegetable oils such as sunflower oil, and K from green leafy vegetables.
steps: A. Vitamin A: carrots are rich in $\beta$-carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A (retinol). So A → IV.
B. Vitamin $B_{12}$ (cyanocobalamin, contains Co): it is made only by microbes and is found almost entirely in animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and curd. Plant foods are not a source. So B → I.
C. Vitamin E (tocopherols): vegetable oils such as sunflower and wheat-germ oil are the classic sources. So C → II.
D. Vitamin K (phylloquinone): green leafy vegetables are the main source. It is needed for blood clotting. So D → III.
The matching is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III, which is option (2). This agrees with the NTA key.
why_not_others: Option (3) pairs $B_{12}$ with sunflower oil and E with meat, but $B_{12}$ is absent from plant oils. Options (1) and (4) wrongly link vitamin A to sunflower oil or leafy greens instead of carrots.
common_trap: Students sometimes swap vitamins E and K, or assume $B_{12}$ can come from plant oils, forgetting that $B_{12}$ is essentially found only in animal products.
time_saving_tip: Fix vitamin A to carrots first. That eliminates options (1) and (4). Then $B_{12}$ → meat separates option (2) from option (3) immediately.
